strengths: Novel trajectory-free training objective based on Mean Flow consistency condition enables training on standard MLFF datasets without expensive trajectory generation
Rigorous mathematical framework with proper derivation of consistency condition from Hamiltonian mechanics principles
Comprehensive experimental validation across diverse systems (1D potentials, N-body gravity, MD17 molecules, peptides) with thorough ablations and multiple evaluation metrics
Significant practical speedups (18-20×) demonstrated while maintaining simulation accuracy and structural observables
Continuous-time model supporting arbitrary timesteps at inference (major advantage over fixed-timestep prior methods)
Efficient implementation with only ~30% overhead vs standard MLFF training using Jacobian-vector products
Transparent and honest discussion of limitations including instabilities, approximate physical conservation, and architectural trade-offs
Excellent reproducibility with detailed algorithms, hyperparameters, and implementation details provided
weaknesses: Inference filters for energy and angular momentum conservation are necessary for stability, indicating learned maps have systematic errors and don't truly respect conservation laws
Unexplained instability around ∆t≈10 fs for alanine dipeptide that doesn't correlate with one-step prediction error, limiting practical timestep selection
Non-equivariant architecture requires data augmentation with random rotations and random rotation filtering during inference—pragmatic but imperfect solution
Trade-off between force accuracy and time consistency: HFM has notably worse instantaneous force MAE than MLFF baseline (e.g., Table 8: 4.4 vs 3.8 meV/Å for aspirin)
Limited scope: largest tested system is 21-atom alanine dipeptide; scalability to realistic protein systems and long-timescale sampling remains undemonstrated
Stop-gradient approximation in loss function avoids expensive higher-order derivatives but impact on convergence and model quality compared to full optimization unclear
Sensitivity to thermostat choice: Nosé-Hoover thermostat produces poor results (Table 10) due to energy equipartition failures; practical constraint if thermostat choice is constrained
Semi-group property analysis (Appendix G.8) shows consistency breaks down beyond ~4 fs, raising questions about validity at claimed 9 fs timesteps

strengths: Novel theoretical framework: Creative adaptation of mean flow consistency conditions from generative modeling to deterministic Hamiltonian dynamics with sound mathematical derivation
Practical training advantage: Trajectory-free training on decorrelated (x, f) samples using widely available MLFF datasets eliminates expensive trajectory generation requirement
Temporal flexibility: Supports arbitrary timesteps ∆t ∈ [0, ∆t_max], elegantly unifying instantaneous force prediction with large-step integration in single model
Comprehensive experimental scope: Diverse validation from toy systems through realistic MD (MD17 molecules, 1 ms alanine dipeptide simulation)
Sophisticated conservation approach: Coupled energy-angular momentum optimization via closed-form constrained optimization is more principled than sequential corrections
Reproducibility support: Extensive implementation details, algorithms, hyperparameters, and ablations in appendices facilitate verification
weaknesses: Critical stability issues inadequately addressed: Table 15 shows catastrophic failure at ∆t=10 fs for alanine dipeptide (PMF error 0.048→29.676, MJS 0.0045→0.5380). Practical usable range is ∆t≤9 fs, not advertised ∆t_max=15 fs. Root cause analysis, workarounds, and failure mode guidance are absent

Fundamental Hamiltonian structure not learned: Non-conservative force predictions by design requiring three post-hoc inference filters. Method learns approximate dynamics needing retroactive corrections rather than true symplectic/energy-conserving maps. Thermostat coupling issues (Table 10: Nosé-Hoover artifacts) indicate fundamental limitations

Incomplete baseline comparisons: Main recent competitor FlashMD (Bigi et al. 2025a) is extensively cited but never experimentally compared on same datasets. Only one generative baseline (ScoreMD) with limited discussion. Cannot assess relative standing

Modest performance gains not justifying complexity: ~18× wall clock speedup (Table 7) requires 50-hour training, complex inference pipeline (3 filters, rotation augmentation), and careful thermostat selection. Missing discussion of when this approach is preferable to MLFF + advanced integrators

Stop-gradient training violates theoretical assumptions: Loss derived assuming full gradient flow, but implementation uses stop-gradient on target (Section 4.2). This breaks mathematical consistency condition. Impact on convergence analysis is missing; trade-offs not rigorously examined

Inconsistency between one-step error and long-time accuracy: Figure 18 shows consistency error comparable to Velocity Verlet only to ~4 fs, yet simulations succeed at ∆t=9 fs. Why does semi-group property violation at large ∆t not cause failure? Mechanism unclear and unexplored

Scalability not demonstrated: Experiments limited to molecules ≤22 atoms. Training times substantial (3d12h for alanine dipeptide). No experiments on proteins, complexes, or realistic large systems. Scalability to practical MD applications unclear

Thermostat sensitivity and robustness concerns: Results vary significantly by thermostat choice (Tables 1, 9, 10). Nosé-Hoover thermostat produces severe artifacts (MAE up to 0.695). Issue acknowledged but not investigated; practitioners lack clear guidance

Non-equivariant architecture with workarounds: Translation-invariant Transformer is not rotationally equivariant despite claims. Requires random rotation augmentation during training (Algorithm 2) and inference (Algorithms 3-4)—architectural patch rather than principled solution

Momentum sampling assumptions unexplored: Method requires Maxwell-Boltzmann momentum sampling justified for separable Hamiltonians. No sensitivity analysis for different temperatures; coupling between momentum sampling and accuracy is unexamined

strengths: Novel trajectory-free training objective elegantly addresses a real bottleneck in molecular dynamics by deriving consistency conditions from instantaneous force labels alone, with rigorous mathematical justification (Appendix C)

Practical advantages over prior trajectory-based methods: eliminates expensive synthetic trajectory generation, trains directly on standard MLFF datasets, maintains unified force field + integrator in single model, supports arbitrary inference timesteps

Comprehensive experimental validation across diverse systems (toy potentials, N-body, MD17, peptides) with multiple evaluation metrics, extensive ablations, and long-timescale simulations (1 ms) demonstrating 18× timestep improvements

Exceptional reproducibility with detailed algorithms, complete hyperparameter specifications, implementation details, standard datasets, and promised code release enabling straightforward reproduction

Honest treatment of limitations including Lyapunov constraints on chaotic systems, verification that inference filters don't artificially stabilize incorrect trajectories (Fig. 21), and explicit documentation of failure modes (Δt ≈ 10 fs instability for alanine dipeptide)

Physical correctness demonstrated through coupled energy/angular momentum conservation (Appendix B.3), semi-group property analysis (Appendix G.8), and verification that spectral properties persist without filters (Fig. 20)
Clear, well-structured presentation with excellent figures and thoughtful positioning relative to flow matching and generative modeling frameworks
weaknesses: Scope limitations: restricted to separable Hamiltonians, experiments on small molecules (~20 atoms), scalability to large proteins unclear, applicability to diverse force field types unexplored

Unresolved stability issues including observed instability at Δt ≈ 10 fs for alanine dipeptide, fundamental hard limits from Lyapunov exponents in chaotic systems, and statement that optimization becomes 'increasingly challenging' at larger timesteps without mechanistic explanation

Model dependence on inference corrections: while verified not to artificially stabilize (Fig. 21), requires post-hoc energy/momentum adjustments not built into architecture, auxiliary MLFF calls increase inference cost, and symplectic properties not guaranteed

Incomplete ablation of core method: force matching component analyzed (Table 8) but force MAE degradation vs. standard MLFFs accepted without deep justification; critical hyperparameter q_Δt=0 = 0.75 and mixture distribution q(τ) = 0.98B(1,2) + 0.02U(0,1) appear ad-hoc
Stop-gradient approximation (Section 4.2) is practical simplification but theoretically impure—impact on convergence and accuracy not quantified
Limited baseline comparisons: no direct quantitative comparison with FlashMD or other recent large-timestep methods; ScoreMD comparison only on paracetamol; MLFF baselines could be more diverse
Generalization concerns: limited evidence beyond small organic molecules, sparse data regime tested only once, unclear robustness to different ab-initio sources or out-of-distribution scenarios

Inference pipeline complexity (drift removal + random rotation + coupled conservation + optional thermostat) and need for rotation augmentation despite translation-invariant architecture suggest approximate rather than principled equivariance

strengths: Sound mathematical framework with rigorous derivation of trajectory-free consistency condition and proof of sufficiency
Novel practical contribution: trajectory-free training enables use of standard MLFF datasets, eliminating expensive trajectory generation bottleneck
Comprehensive experimental validation across diverse systems (classical mechanics, MD17, MD22, peptides, proteins) with honest acknowledgment of limitations
Convincing demonstration of data efficiency advantages over trajectory-matching baselines (G.14) in low-data regimes
Well-justified implementation choices: Jacobian-vector products, stop-gradient formulation (~30% overhead), coupled conservation filters tested to not artificially stabilize invalid dynamics
Single model functions as both force field and large-timestep integrator, enabling flexible timestep selection at inference
Extensive ablations and supplementary analysis (46 pages) thoroughly exploring design choices and system behavior
weaknesses: Fundamental non-conservatism of learned maps requires post-hoc inference filters; while these don't artificially enable arbitrary timesteps, they represent departure from true Hamiltonian mechanics and add implementation complexity

Unexplained stability issues at specific timesteps (e.g., ∆t≈10 fs in alanine dipeptide) despite low one-step errors; semi-group property violated significantly beyond 4 fs (Fig 19) while larger timesteps still employed

Modest empirical speedups: Table 9 shows 2.5× improvement over SchNet; when accounting for energy correction overhead, speedup advantage diminishes; '10-20× speedup' claim in abstract not well-supported by results
Limited generalizability: Nosé-Hoover thermostat shows clear artifacts (Table 12); force prediction error increases with ∆t (Table 10); only Langevin thermostat fully robust
Stop-gradient approximation reduces accuracy for speed; You et al. (2026) suggests full gradients yield better results, but trade-off not thoroughly analyzed
Primary baseline comparisons (MLFF+VV, ScoreMD) in main paper; direct comparison with FlashMD/TrajCast relegated to appendix; key ablations and failure analysis in appendices rather than main text

Momentum sampling during training requires Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution assumptions not necessarily reflective of actual training data; introduces hyperparameters and assumptions about data distribution
